They turned, but in the next instant the sleigh was surrounded by wolves. Gray shapes darted past them, white teeth gleamed in gaping jaws, and fiery eyes shone. They howled with hunger and bloodlust. The gleaming teeth were ready to sink into soft human flesh. The wolves leaped up at Don Juan and fastened themselves to the harness. Anna sat wondering whether they would devour them completely or whether anything would remain, so that the next morning people would find mangled limbs on the trampled, bloody snow.

“Our lives are at stake now,” she said, bent down, and seized Tancred by the scruff of the neck.

“Let him be, it is no use! It is not for the dog’s sake that the wolves are abroad tonight.”

With that, Gösta drove into the courtyard at Berga, but the wolves pursued him all the way to the steps. He had to fend them off with the whip.

“Anna,” he said when they stopped by the steps, “God did not will it. Keep up a brave face now, if you are the woman I take you for; keep up a brave face!”

Those inside heard the jingling of the bells and came out.

“He has her,” they cried, “he has her! Long live Gösta Berling!” And the newcomers were snatched from embrace to embrace.

Not many questions were asked. The night was far advanced, the travelers were shaken by their perilous journey and needed rest. It was enough, after all, that Anna had come.

All was well. Only Corinne and the green traveling sash, Mamsell Ulrika’s cherished gift, had been destroyed.

*

The whole house slept. Then Gösta rose, dressed, and stole outside. Quite unnoticed, he took Don Juan from the stable, harnessed him to the sleigh, and intended to set off. Then Anna Stjärnhök came out of the house.

“I heard you go out,” she said. “So I too got up. I am ready to travel with you.”

He went up to her and took her hand.

“Do you not understand it even yet? It cannot be. God does not will it. Listen now, and try to understand! I was here at noon and saw their misery over your faithlessness. Then I went to Borg to bring you back to Ferdinand. But I have always been a wretch and will never be anything else. I betrayed him and kept you for myself. There is an old woman here who believes that I shall become a man. I betrayed her. And another poor old creature is willing to freeze and starve here merely so that she may die among friends, but I stood ready to let the wicked Sintram take her home. You were beautiful and the sin was sweet. Gösta Berling is so easily tempted. Oh, what a wretch I am!—I know how they love their home, those people in there, yet only a moment ago I stood ready to abandon it to pillage. I forgot everything for your sake; you were so sweet in your love. But now, Anna, now that I have seen their joy, I will not keep you; no, I will not. You are the one who would have made a human being of me, but I may not keep you. Oh, my beloved! He up above toys with our wills. Now it is time for us to bow beneath the chastening hand. Say that from this day onward you will take your burden upon you! All those inside rely upon you. Say that you will stay with them and become their support and aid! If you love me, if you wish to ease my deep sorrow, then promise me this! My beloved, is your heart so great that it can conquer itself and smile as it does so?”

She received the command of renunciation with rapture.

“I shall do as you wish: sacrifice myself and smile as I do so.”

“And not hate my poor friends?”

She smiled mournfully.

“As long as I love you, I shall love them.”

“Only now do I know what kind of woman you are. It is hard to go away from you.”

“Farewell, Gösta! Go now with God! My love shall not entice you into sin.”

She turned to go inside. He followed her.

“Will you soon forget me?”

“Go now, Gösta! We are only human.”

He threw himself down into the sleigh, but then she came back.

“Are you not thinking of the wolves?”

“It is precisely of them that I am thinking, but they have done their work. They have no further business with me tonight.”

Once more he stretched out his arms toward her, but Don Juan grew impatient and dashed off. He did not take hold of the reins. He sat facing backward and looked back. Then he leaned against the side of the sleigh and wept like one in despair.

“I possessed happiness and drove her away from me. I myself drove her away from me. Why did I not keep her?”

Ah, Gösta Berling, strongest and weakest among men!

CHAPTER FIVE.

La cachucha.

Warhorse, warhorse! You old one who now stand tethered in the field, do you remember your youth?

Do you remember the day of battle, you brave one? You charged forward as though borne on wings, your rider streamed above you like flickering flames, and on your black breast spatters of blood gleamed amid frothing foam. In trappings of gold you charged forward, and the ground thundered beneath you. You trembled with joy, you brave one. Ah, how beautiful you were!

It is a gray twilight hour up in the Cavaliers’ Wing. In the large room the cavaliers’ red-painted chests stand along the walls, and their Sunday clothes hang from hooks in the corner. The glow of the fire from the open hearth plays over whitewashed walls and yellow-checkered curtains that conceal the wall-bed cupboards. The Cavaliers’ Wing is no royal chamber, no seraglio with upholstered divans and soft cushions.

But inside, Lilliecrona’s violin can be heard. He is playing La cachucha in the twilight. Over and over again he plays it.

Cut the strings, break the bow to pieces! Why does he play this accursed dance? Why does he play it when Örneclou, the ensign, is lying ill this very moment in agonies of gout so severe that he cannot move in his bed? No, snatch the violin from him and hurl it against the wall if he will not stop!

La cachucha—is it for us, master? Is it to be danced over the swaying floorboards of the Cavaliers’ Wing, between narrow walls blackened by smoke and greasy with grime, beneath this low ceiling? Woe to you, the way you play!

La cachucha—is it for us, for us cavaliers? Outside, the snowstorm howls. Do you intend to teach the flakes to dance in time; are you playing for the light-footed children of the blizzard?

Women’s bodies trembling with the pulsebeats of hot blood, little soot-stained hands that have flung aside the cooking pot to seize the castanets, bare feet beneath kilted-up skirts, a courtyard paved with chips of marble, crouching Gypsies with bagpipe and tambourine, Moorish arcades, moonlight, and black eyes—do you have all this, master? Otherwise, let the violin rest!

Cavaliers are drying their wet clothes before the fire. Are they to whirl about in high boots with iron-shod heels and soles an inch thick? Through snow an ell deep they have waded all day to reach the bear’s den. Do you think they are to dance in wet, steaming homespun clothes, with the shaggy bear as their partner?
